title: Evaluation of aortic calcification and endovascular therapy of aortic lesions
summary: The average prevalence of peripheral arterial occlusive disease is estimated at 3-10%. It increases to 15-20% in people over 80 years of age. If the abdominal aorta is involved, it can be affected either in isolation or in combination with the iliac arteries. In addition, in rare cases there is isolated severe calcification of the abdominal aorta. This finding is referred to as a coral reef aorta. If the above-mentioned lesions lead to high-grade narrowing of the arterial pathway, this results in multiple symptoms such as Lower limb ischaemia, arterial hypertension, visceral ischaemia and others. There is no conclusive evidence regarding the best treatment for aortic stenoses. While in the past these complex lesions were always treated surgically, the primary and secondary open rates after endovascular treatment of these lesions have improved significantly due to numerous technical developments. Overall, the role of endovascular treatment of aortic lesions has not been conclusively clarified and there is a lack of large randomised comparative studies between endovascular and open surgical procedures. The aim of this retrospective, monocentric study is to evaluate the quality of the results of aortic endovascular interventions.

interventions.name: Patients with interventions of the abdominal aorta or the aorta involving the iliac arteries who were treated at the University Medical Centre Freiburg at the University Heart Centre on the Bad Krozingen campus.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients with interventions of the abdominal aorta or the aorta involving the iliac arteries who were treated at the University Medical Centre Freiburg at the University Heart Centre on the Bad Krozingen campus
Exclusion criteria:
- Patients who have not been treated aortally or aorto-iliacally
- Patients who have undergone interventional treatment due to an aneurysm of the aorta or the aorta involving the iliac arteries.
